opus-5.5.text:
I think the main advantage is that we try to look at Physical AI as a full-stack problem, and we try to support developers at every layer of that stack.

If you think about what it takes to build a physical AI system, whether it's a robot, an autonomous vehicle, or a smart factory, you really need three kinds of computers. You need a computer to train the AI model, and that's the data center side, our GPUs and systems like DGX. Then you need a computer to simulate and generate data, because in the physical world, data is very expensive and very hard to collect. You can't just crawl the internet for robot interaction data the way you can for text. So we built platforms like Omniverse, and more recently Cosmos, our world foundation models, to help developers generate synthetic data and test their policies in simulation before they go to the real world. And then the third computer is the one that sits inside the robot or the car, which is our Jetson and DRIVE platforms. So we can support developers from training to simulation to deployment.

The second advantage, I would say, is that we are very committed to an open ecosystem. For Cosmos, for example, we released the models with open weights and a permissive license, because we believe Physical AI is still at a very early stage. No single company is going to solve it alone. We want to give researchers and startups a strong starting point, so they don't need to spend tens of millions of dollars just to pretrain a world model from scratch. They can take our model and post-train it for their own robot, their own environment, their own use case.

And the third thing is that we have a lot of accumulated expertise. NVIDIA has been doing graphics and simulation for decades, physics simulation, rendering, and we've been doing deep learning research for more than ten years. My own team works on generative AI, and a lot of that came from work on image and video generation. When you put those together, graphics, simulation, generative models, and accelerated computing, it turns out they're exactly the ingredients you need for Physical AI. So in some sense, we've been preparing for this moment for a long time, even if we didn't always call it Physical AI.

So I would summarize it as: full-stack computing, an open platform, and deep expertise in both simulation and generative AI. Our goal is really to be the platform that helps everyone else build their physical AI systems faster.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Nvidia’s training, simulation, and deployment platforms but does not attribute lower GPU compute costs to Nvidia manufacturing GPUs itself.

r002.rationale: The candidate says Nvidia supports an open ecosystem and aims to help others build systems faster, but does not explain that customers collaborate because Nvidia will not replicate or displace their products.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the biggest advantage is that Nvidia is really a full-stack company, and Physical AI needs the full stack more than almost any other area of AI.

Let me explain what I mean. When you build a robot or an autonomous vehicle, you need three computers, not one. You need a computer to train the model, which is the DGX. You need a computer to simulate and generate data, which is what we do with Omniverse and Cosmos. And you need a computer that runs inside the robot itself, which is Jetson and Thor. Very few companies can offer all three, and we designed them to work together so a developer does not have to stitch everything by themselves.

The second advantage is data. In language, the internet gives you trillions of tokens for free. In Physical AI, there is no internet of robot experience. Collecting data with real robots is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. So we invest heavily in simulation and in world foundation models. Cosmos, for example, lets a developer take a small amount of real data and generate many physically plausible variations, with different lighting, weather, object placement. That multiplies what the developer has and helps the policy generalize. I think this is where we spend a lot of our research energy, because it is the real bottleneck.

Third, we open a lot of this up. We release the models, the weights, the tools. Our goal is not to build the robot ourselves. Our goal is to make every robotics company, big or small, able to build on top of us. If a startup with ten people can train and deploy a capable humanoid policy using our stack, that is a success for us.

And finally, I would say the ecosystem. CUDA has been around for almost twenty years, so the developer community, the libraries, and the know-how are already there. Physical AI developers inherit all of that on day one.

r002.rationale: It says Nvidia aims to enable robotics companies rather than build robots itself, but does not say this makes customers more willing to collaborate or that Nvidia avoids replicating and displacing their products.

astra-6.text:
I think Nvidia’s main advantage is that we can support the whole development process. Physical AI isn’t just about training a model. Developers need to generate data, test how a system interacts with the world, and then run it on a robot with real-time constraints.

We bring together accelerated computing, simulation, and deployment tools. That lets developers connect those stages more easily: train a model, evaluate it in simulation, learn from the failures, and improve it before testing on hardware.

The ecosystem is also important. Robotics requires expertise across many areas, so having shared tools and a platform that developers and partners can build on helps teams spend more time solving their particular problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Nvidia’s main advantage is that it can support the entire development cycle for Physical AI. You need to train models, test them in simulation, and then deploy them on a robot or another physical system. Having those pieces work together makes the developer’s job much easier.

Simulation is especially important because collecting data in the real world is expensive, and some situations are difficult or unsafe to reproduce. Developers need a way to generate diverse scenarios, evaluate their models, and iterate before putting a system into the real world.

Then there’s the computing platform and the software ecosystem around it. The value is more than raw performance—it’s giving researchers and developers tools that work together, so they can spend more time solving their application problems.
